summary: A humorous April 1 memo composed of letters that imagine a possible future viewed from the 21st century. It is informational and not a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st RFC presents emails supposedly sent from the year 2023. The correspondents discuss a fictional future and look back on Internet history, while the memo warns readers not to rely on the letters' accuracy.

questions: april first rfc letters from the future
subtitle: A fictional set of future letters about Internet history and growth.

tldr.problem: The memo asks readers to imagine how the Internet might look from a future vantage point.
tldr.mechanism: It presents a sequence of emails supposedly written in 2023 by correspondents on Mars and the Moon, discussing imagined technology and accounts of earlier Internet history.
tldr.outcome: The exchange uses a fictional future to reflect on Internet growth, IPng design, and other technical and policy questions.

today: RFC 1607 is an Informational April 1st document presenting a fictional future correspondence. Its opening note cautions that the letters' accuracy cannot be vouched for.

sections.title: The Time-Capsule Premise
sections.content:
The RFC frames its body as letters discovered in September 1993 in a reverse time capsule apparently sent from 2023. The author says he cannot vouch for the letters' accuracy and warns readers to be careful about acting on the future history they contain.

The letters describe correspondents living or working on Mars, the Moon, and Earth, with imagined communications and research technology.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo presents a made-up correspondence from 2023. Its opening note says the author cannot confirm that the letters are accurate.

sections.title: The Letters' View of Internet History
sections.content:
One correspondent recounts a history of packet networking, ARPANET, TCP/IP, and the growth of connected networks. Another describes finding old RFCs and discusses the IPng design debates of 1991–1994 as seen from the imagined future.

Later letters describe the fictional correspondents' account of network growth, new access methods, multimedia, and policy questions. These are statements within the imagined exchange, not claims verified by the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The correspondents tell a story about how networks grew and discuss the IPng debates. The RFC presents that story as future correspondence, not as a verified report.

sections.title: Speculation and Open Questions
sections.content: The final comments note that the letters leave loose ends and that technical, policy, and economic questions remain. The memo closes by inviting speculation about the future described in the exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The correspondence ends without resolving every question. The memo leaves the future it describes open to speculation.
